name: Travelers
headline: An insurer whose policyholder float has been a net gain, not a cost, in every year of a decade.
what_it_does: Travelers sells property and casualty insurance through three segments: Business Insurance, Bond and Specialty Insurance, and Personal Insurance. It collects premiums up front and invests them until claims are paid, holding about $81 billion of such float in mid-2026. It has no life-insurance or other non-insurance business.
why_it_passed: It made an underwriting profit in every one of ten years, so the float cost less than nothing: an average of -3.06% from 2021 to 2025, against a 30-year US Treasury rate of 3.69%.
That held through catastrophe years of $2.99 billion to $3.69 billion in 2023 to 2025.
Its return on equity has been in the mid-teens over five years, earned with an underwriting profit on top of investment income.
No sign of dishonesty was found, the accounts and reserve tables are clear, and capital not needed is returned to owners.
why_not_now: At $360.70 a share, the price is at the top of the analysis's value range of $151 to $366. At that price a buyer would earn about 4% a year before growth, below the 5.66% of a 30-year US Treasury bond and far below the roughly 10% the framework requires.
watch: It is not a structural moat: Travelers is neither the low-cost operator nor the best underwriter against its rivals, and trails Chubb, Berkley and Hartford's commercial business.
Reserve releases have run high while the company buys back its own stock, and the buybacks name no price and were made above the bottom of the value range.
Pay depends on a return-on-equity target and adjusted figures, and the 2024 and 2025 accident years have yet to mature as booked.
